catalog_quote: 2.1 Word structure Regarding word structure, Va does not exhibit the typical Mon-Khmer sesquisyllabic pattern consisting of a phonologically weak minor syllable followed by a full-fledged major syllable. Instead, the language has become completely monosyllabic. ... 2.2.3 Tone Va distinguishes three tonal levels: high, mid, and low. What matters in this system is relative pitch register, as the actual pitch contours vary according to syllable type and the position of a syllable inside a word. For example, all tones are falling in syllables ending in -h, and level in syllables ending in -ʔ. It is therefore misleading to assign steady tone letters (as in Zhou 1988) or tone numerals (as in Liu 2006) to underlying tones in Va. ... [§4] Va has cast off the original PWL sesquisyllablic word structure in favor of a fully monosyllabic one, and, caught “in the great wave of tonal splits that swept across Southeast Asia and the Far East some centuries ago” (Gedney 1985: 117), invoked phonemic tones to compensate for lost syllable canons and coalesced articulation manners of onset consonants.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Va (Yingla/Xiyun) has no sesquisyllables: every word is a single syllable C(C)(C)V(V)(C) carrying one of three level tones (high, mid, low). The source makes no statement about stress at all; word stress is moot in a fully monosyllabic tone language.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only marginal structure noted is the -CC coda in the onomatopoeic miáwŋ 'meow'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word = syllable: the language is described as completely monosyllabic, so there is no word-internal stress placement to state; tone (three pitch registers) is the word-level prosodic contrast. Contour realisation is said to vary with syllable type and with the syllable's position in the (compound/phrasal) word, which is the only remark on positional prominence; nothing on compound or phrase stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 2018 describes the Va of Yingla 英臘 (zoŋráʔ) village, Wenggake 翁嘎科 Township, Ximeng 西盟 County, Pu'er, Yunnan; the Glottolog name 'Xiyun Va' comes from the type locality Xiyun 細允 hamlet, Donggang village, Donghui Township, Lancang County (Zhou 1988; Zhou et al. 2004). Sun (fn. 3) states the Xiyun and Yingla varieties are 'phonologically very similar' (differences: PWL *r- > ɣ in Xiyun vs r in Yingla; stop epenthesis in nasal+liquid clusters in Yingla only), so both fall under xiyu1235 (Glottolog's reference record lists the language as 'Xiyun = Va'). Va is distinct from Lavïa (Masan), which Glottolog keeps under Awa [vwa]; the open-access Sun 2020 Lavïa paper saved here is about that other language and must not be used for xiyu1235.

sources.note: Describes a DIFFERENT language (Lavïa = Masan variety of Chinese 'Awa' [vwa]). p. 286: 'Masan and Xiyun are distinct Wa-Lawa languages, to be renamed Lavïa (la-vɨɒʔ) and Va (vàʔ; Sun 2018b)'; fn. 24 p. 306: 'the Wa-Lawa language Vaʔ' makes contrastive use of tones. For Lavïa itself (not the target): sesquisyllabic, 'a phonologically reduced minor syllable precedes a stressed major syllable. The iambic stress pattern also carries over to compound words' (p. 287).
